followUps:
The change-making algorithm lives in its own small collaborator (a ChangeMaker or the CoinBox), not inside any state class, because it is pure logic that several states and tests need. It takes the coin inventory and an amount and returns a coin list or impossible.

Greedy (largest coin first) is correct for canonical coin sets such as 1, 5, 10, 25, but fails for odd sets: coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6 gives greedy 4+1+1 (3 coins) while 3+3 needs 2. With limited stock use DP or backtracking. Call it before dispensing so a sale is refused if change cannot be made.

You must refund the customer and report the fault, because the machine took money for nothing. This is why the order is: plan change, move to a persisted DISPENSING state, run the motor, and only commit the sale when the sensor confirms the product dropped.

If the motor jams, the machine fires a DISPENSE_FAILED event: credit goes back to escrow (or coins are returned), the slot is flagged as faulty, stock is not decremented, and the state returns to IDLE or SOLD_OUT. Money is only moved from escrow to the cash box at commit, so there is nothing to undo.

code.title: Two-state machine as a transition table
code.python:
# Two states, no per-state behaviour: an enum-style transition table is enough (no State classes)
TABLE = {("LOCKED", "coin"): "UNLOCKED", ("LOCKED", "push"): "LOCKED",
         ("UNLOCKED", "push"): "LOCKED", ("UNLOCKED", "coin"): "UNLOCKED"}
state = "LOCKED"
for event in ["push", "coin", "coin", "push", "push"]:
    nxt = TABLE[(state, event)]              # one lookup replaces a class per state
    print("%-9s + %-4s -> %s" % (state, event, nxt))
    state = nxt
print("final:", state)

followUps:
With an enum and a transition table the whole machine is data: one map from (state, event) to the next state, as in the program above. A turnstile needs only four entries and a loop.

With State classes each state is a class that owns the behaviour for every event:

class Locked implements State {
  State coin(Ctx c) { return new Unlocked(); }
  State push(Ctx c) { return this; }
}

The table is shorter and easier to scan for two or three states. The classes win once states need their own fields, fees or hardware actions, because each behaviour then has one home instead of a growing switch.

Sealed types with exhaustive matching give you the safety of State classes with the compactness of a table: the compiler refuses to build until every state is handled.

In Java 21 a sealed interface State with record cases and a switch over it fails to compile if you add Maintenance and forget a branch. That removes the main weakness of an enum plus switch (a silently missed case). It also keeps behaviour in one function, so you can see all transitions side by side. Choose classes when each state carries lots of behaviour or hardware logic; choose sealed types when states are mostly data and transitions are pure functions.

code.title: Elevator car as a single state field

followUps:
The door-obstruction rule lives in the DOORS_OPEN state, because only that state knows what to do with a sensor event while the doors are open or closing.

On each tick DOORS_OPEN checks the sensor first: if blocked, it resets the door timer to its full value and stays open; if clear, it counts down and only at zero moves to IDLE. Example with a 3-tick timer: tick 1 timer 2, tick 2 sensor blocked so timer resets to 3, then 3 clear ticks, then close. Keeping it there means MOVING_* can never run while the doors are open, so no other state needs to know the rule.

Add a new state and one event handler, and leave the existing states alone: the cleanest way is a hierarchy or a global override in the context, not edits in every state.

Create a FireRecall state that clears all stops, sends the car to the ground floor, opens the doors and then rejects all calls. Then let the context check a FIRE event before delegating: if (event == FIRE) { setState(new FireRecall()); return; }. The old states stay untouched, which is the open-closed principle. With a hierarchical machine you instead put FIRE once on the parent state that holds IDLE, MOVING and DOORS_OPEN.

code.title: FCFS vs SSTF vs SCAN vs LOOK travel
code.python:
# Total floors travelled by FCFS, SSTF, SCAN and LOOK (start floor 5 going up, top floor 9)
START, TOP = 5, 9
reqs = [8, 2, 6, 1, 4]

def travel(path):
    pos, total = START, 0
    for f in path:
        total += abs(f - pos)
        pos = f
    return total

def sstf(r):
    left, pos, out = list(r), START, []
    while left:
        nxt = min(left, key=lambda f: (abs(f - pos), -f))  # nearest; ties go higher
        left.remove(nxt); out.append(nxt); pos = nxt
    return out

up = sorted(f for f in reqs if f >= START)
down = sorted((f for f in reqs if f < START), reverse=True)
paths = {"FCFS": reqs, "SSTF": sstf(reqs),
         "SCAN": up + [TOP] + down,  # sweeps to the end floor before reversing
         "LOOK": up + down}          # reverses at the last request
print("start", START, "requests", reqs)
for name, p in paths.items():
    print(name, p, "->", travel(p), "floors")

followUps:
LOOK cannot starve a request because the car only reverses after serving every request ahead of it, and each sweep ends after a bounded number of floors.

Take a request at floor f. If the car is moving toward f, it reaches f within one sweep (at most F floors, where F is the number of floors) because it never skips a requested floor in its direction. If the car is moving away, it turns around once the last request in that direction is done, and then reaches f on the return sweep. New requests behind the car wait for the next sweep but cannot delay f, so waiting is at most about two sweeps (2F floors of travel). SSTF has no such bound, since nearer requests can keep arriving.

C-LOOK is LOOK that only serves requests while moving in one direction: after the last request it jumps back to the lowest waiting request and sweeps up again, like a circular list.

It is fairer because waiting time is more uniform. In plain LOOK a request near the middle is served after about half a sweep on average, but a request at an end floor can be served twice in a row while the middle waits. Example: floors 1 to 10, car at 5 going up, requests 2 and 9: LOOK serves 9 then 2. C-LOOK also serves 9, then jumps to 2, then continues upward. The cost is the jump, which is wasted travel but cheap for disks; for elevators the empty return trip is why LOOK is more common.

code.title: Cost-based hall call dispatch

followUps:
Nearest by distance ignores direction, load, and whether a car can serve the call at all, so it often gives a worse wait than a car that is a bit further away.

In the program above, car D is closest (distance 0) but is in maintenance, so it cannot take the call. Car C is one floor away but is going down and must finish its sweep first, so its real cost is 21. Car A is 5 floors away but idle with no stops, so it arrives soonest (cost 5). Nearest-by-distance also piles calls on one car, which then stops at every floor. A cost function (time to reach plus a penalty per assigned stop) fixes all of this.

Make the dispatcher a Strategy and swap it on a schedule, so the car state machines are not touched at all.

Define DispatchStrategy.assign(call, cars). Keep CostDispatch as the default and add ZonedDispatch, where each car owns a band of floors (for example cars 1 and 2 serve floors 1 to 10 and cars 3 and 4 serve 11 to 20) during up-peak, when most calls start in the lobby. A scheduler or building-mode flag does dispatcher = zoned at 9:00 and switches back at 10:00. Calls already assigned finish normally; only new calls use the new strategy.

code.title: Idempotent debit and reversal by txnId
code.python:
# Idempotent bank: the txnId makes retried debits and reversals harmless
class Bank:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance
        self.txns = {}                      # txnId -> "DEBITED" or "REVERSED" (tombstone)

    def debit(self, txn, amount):
        state = self.txns.get(txn)
        if state == "REVERSED":
            return "REFUSED"                # late debit after a reversal
        if state is None:
            self.balance -= amount
            self.txns[txn] = "DEBITED"
        return "OK"                         # repeat of the same id changes nothing

    def reverse(self, txn, amount):
        if self.txns.get(txn) == "DEBITED":
            self.balance += amount
        self.txns[txn] = "REVERSED"         # keep a tombstone even if never seen
        return "OK"

bank = Bank(100)
print("start balance", bank.balance)
print("debit t1 50 ->", bank.debit("t1", 50), bank.balance)
print("debit t1 50 (retry) ->", bank.debit("t1", 50), bank.balance)
print("dispenser jammed, no cash given")
print("reverse t1 ->", bank.reverse("t1", 50), bank.balance)
print("reverse t1 (retry) ->", bank.reverse("t1", 50), bank.balance)
print("late debit t1 ->", bank.debit("t1", 50), bank.balance)

followUps:
The bank must store, for every transaction id, what it did and its outcome, in the same atomic write as the balance change, so a repeat finds the old result instead of acting twice.

A row looks like (txnId, cardId, amount, status, createdAt) with status DEBITED or REVERSED, and a unique key on txnId. Debit and reversal happen in one database transaction with the balance update. A repeated debit finds the row and returns the saved result; a reversal marks it REVERSED. Keep the rows for longer than the longest possible retry window (for example 30 days), otherwise an old retry looks new and charges twice.

The ATM keeps resending it, because the reversal is journaled as pending until the bank acknowledges it. This is why the reversal must be idempotent too.

Steps: the ATM writes REVERSAL_PENDING(txnId) to its journal, sends reverse(txnId), and retries with backoff (say 1 s, 2 s, 4 s) until it receives an ack. If the ATM restarts, replay of the journal finds the pending item and resumes. If the bank never saw the original debit, a reversal still stores a tombstone, so a late-arriving debit with that id is refused. If retries run out, the item is escalated to an operations queue for manual reconciliation.

code.title: PIN counter in session vs ATM field

followUps:
Unblocking must be done by the bank, not the ATM, and only after identity is proven through a second channel and every step is logged.

A safe flow: the customer verifies in a branch (ID check) or through a strong channel such as an app with second-factor confirmation. An authorised staff member or service then sets the card state from BLOCKED to ACTIVE and resets the failed-attempt counter to 0, writing an audit record (who, when, why). Often the card is reissued or the PIN reset, because the PIN may have been guessed. Never expose a self-service reset based only on card number plus date of birth.

A plain string can be read from memory, logs and crash dumps, so the PIN must never exist in clear text in software that a thief or malware could reach.

Real ATMs use an encrypting PIN pad (an EPP), a tamper-resistant device: the keypad encrypts the digits inside the hardware into a PIN block, and the ATM application only ever sees ciphertext that it forwards to the bank. In the model, represent it as an opaque EncryptedPinBlock type with no toString. If a PIN must briefly be held in code, use a char[] and zero it immediately after use, and never log it.

code.title: Check-then-act race fixed with a version CAS
code.python:
# Check-then-act race replayed in a fixed order, then fixed with a version check (CAS)
stock, version, sold = 1, 0, 0
a_stock = stock; b_stock = stock             # both buyers read stock = 1
if a_stock > 0: stock = a_stock - 1; sold += 1   # A passes the guard and writes
if b_stock > 0: stock = b_stock - 1; sold += 1   # B used its stale read too
print("unsafe: stock", stock, "sold", sold)

stock, version, sold = 1, 0, 0
def cas(expected_version, new_stock):
    global stock, version
    if version != expected_version:
        return False                         # someone else committed first
    stock, version = new_stock, version + 1
    return True

a_ver, a_stock = version, stock              # both read the snapshot (version 0)
b_ver, b_stock = version, stock
if a_stock > 0 and cas(a_ver, a_stock - 1): sold += 1
ok = b_stock > 0 and cas(b_ver, b_stock - 1)
print("B first try:", "committed" if ok else "rejected, retry")
if not ok and stock > 0 and cas(version, stock - 1): sold += 1   # retry on fresh data
print("safe: stock", stock, "sold", sold, "version", version)

followUps:
Because another thread could change the state between the read and the write, the snapshot must not change under you: if it did, the CAS would compare against a value that no longer describes what you decided on.

With an immutable snapshot (stock=1, version=7) your decision was made from exactly those values; compareAndSet(old, new) then succeeds only if the reference still points at that same object. If the object were mutable, another thread could change its stock to 0 in place and the reference would still match, so you would sell the last item twice. Immutability also lets the loser safely retry with a fresh snapshot.

For an elevator car I would use a single-threaded event loop (the actor style): one thread owns the car, and all calls, sensor events and timer ticks are queued to it.

The car is physical: its events (floor sensor, door sensor, buttons) arrive in an order that matters, and the state changes constantly. A lock would be held across slow hardware actions, and CAS retries make no sense when you cannot undo a motor move. With a queue the state machine needs no locks, tests are deterministic (feed a list of events), and the one remaining shared point is handing hall calls to the car, which is a thread-safe queue.

code.title: Persist state name and version, recover after crash
code.python:
# Persist the state NAME + version, move to DISPENSING before the side effect, recover after a crash
def show(r):
    return "[%s, %d]" % (r[0], r[1])

table = {}                                   # machineId -> [status, version]  (the "database")

def save(mid, status, expected_version):
    row = table.get(mid)
    current = row[1] if row else None
    if current != expected_version:
        return False                         # optimistic lock: stale writer loses
    table[mid] = [status, expected_version + 1]
    return True

table["m1"] = ["IDLE", 0]
print("insert coin :", save("m1", "HAS_MONEY", 0), show(table["m1"]))
print("select      :", save("m1", "DISPENSING", 1), show(table["m1"]))   # persisted BEFORE the motor runs
print("stale write :", save("m1", "IDLE", 1), "(version 1 is old)")
print("-- crash: memory lost, only the table survives --")

recovery = {"IDLE": "nothing to do", "HAS_MONEY": "refund coins",
            "DISPENSING": "check the motor sensor, refund if unsure"}   # factory keyed by stored name
for mid, (status, ver) in table.items():
    print(mid, "rehydrated as", status, "v%d ->" % ver, recovery[status])
    if status == "DISPENSING":
        save(mid, "IDLE", ver)               # reconcile and finish
print("after recovery:", show(table["m1"]))

followUps:
It solves the problem of doing two things that cannot be one transaction: saving your data and telling other systems about it. Without it you can save and crash before publishing, or publish and then fail to save.

With the outbox you write the state change and an outbox row (the event to publish) in the same database transaction, so both succeed or both fail. A separate relay process reads unsent rows and publishes them, marking them sent. Delivery is at least once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates (use the event id). Example: the vending row moves to DISPENSING and the outbox row DispenseRequested is written together.

Event sourcing fits a vending fleet well for audit and diagnosis, but it adds complexity that a simple status column avoids.

Good: every coin, selection and jam is kept, so you can replay a machine's history, find out why a refund happened and rebuild any past state. Bad: you need snapshots (for example every 100 events) so a machine with a year of events loads quickly; schema changes to old events need versioning; queries such as which machines are low on cola need a separate read model; and replays must not repeat side effects. Use it when audit and money disputes matter; use a status plus version column when they do not.

code.title: Adding a MAINTENANCE state
code.python:
# Adding MAINTENANCE: one new class, one new default method, two small overrides
class State:                                   # default-reject: every cell is "not now" unless overridden
    name = "?"
    def insert(self, m): return "not now"
    def service(self, m): return "not now"
    def finish(self, m): return "not now"
    def restock(self, m, n): return "not now"
    def cancel(self, m): return "not now"

class Idle(State):
    name = "IDLE"
    def insert(self, m): m.state = HasMoney(); return "coin accepted"
    def service(self, m): m.state = Maintenance(); return "service mode"

class SoldOut(State):
    name = "SOLD_OUT"
    def insert(self, m): return "coin returned"
    def service(self, m): m.state = Maintenance(); return "service mode"

class HasMoney(State):                         # keeps the default service(): never open with money in escrow
    name = "HAS_MONEY"
    def cancel(self, m): m.state = Idle(); return "coin returned"

class Maintenance(State):
    name = "MAINTENANCE"
    def insert(self, m): return "coin returned"
    def restock(self, m, n): m.stock += n; return "restocked %d" % n
    def finish(self, m): m.state = Idle() if m.stock > 0 else SoldOut(); return "back in service"

class Machine:
    def __init__(self): self.stock, self.state = 0, SoldOut()

m = Machine()
steps = [("insert", lambda: m.state.insert(m)), ("service", lambda: m.state.service(m)),
         ("insert", lambda: m.state.insert(m)), ("restock 2", lambda: m.state.restock(m, 2)),
         ("finish", lambda: m.state.finish(m)), ("insert", lambda: m.state.insert(m)),
         ("service", lambda: m.state.service(m)), ("cancel", lambda: m.state.cancel(m))]
for label, act in steps:
    print("%-9s -> %s [%s]" % (label, act(), m.state.name))

followUps:
Because a technician opening the machine while a customer's money sits in escrow could take it, or the customer could lose their coins when the machine goes out of service.

In HAS_MONEY, service() keeps the default "not now" answer. The sale must first finish (dispense) or be cancelled (coins returned), and the machine then returns to IDLE, where service() is allowed. Example: customer inserts 2 coins, the technician presses service: refused. The customer presses cancel, 2 coins come back, state is IDLE; now service() works. The program above shows this exact sequence.

Test the whole table: one test per (state, event) cell, generated from a list so none is skipped, and assert both the new state and the side effect.

With 5 states and 5 events that is 25 cells; adding MAINTENANCE and service/finish/restock adds one row and about three columns. Use a parameterised test: [state, event] -> (expectedState, expectedMessage). The expected value for most new cells is "not now, unchanged", and checking that nothing else changed (stock, credit) catches accidental side effects. Add one scenario test for the full path: sold out, service, restock, finish, insert.

code.title: Hierarchical states with event bubbling
code.python:
# Hierarchical states: FIRE is written once on the OPERATIONAL parent and bubbles up from any child
parent = {"IDLE": "OPERATIONAL", "MOVING": "OPERATIONAL", "DOORS_OPEN": "OPERATIONAL",
          "OPERATIONAL": None, "FIRE_RECALL": None}
table = {("IDLE", "call"): "MOVING", ("MOVING", "arrive"): "DOORS_OPEN",
         ("DOORS_OPEN", "close"): "IDLE", ("OPERATIONAL", "FIRE"): "FIRE_RECALL",
         ("FIRE_RECALL", "reset"): "IDLE"}

def chain(s):                                  # state, its parent, grandparent...
    out = []
    while s:
        out.append(s); s = parent[s]
    return out

cur = "IDLE"
for event in ["call", "arrive", "FIRE", "arrive", "reset"]:
    s, target = cur, None
    while s and target is None:                # bubble up until some ancestor handles the event
        target = table.get((s, event)); s = parent[s] if target is None else s
    if target is None:
        print("%-6s: %s ignored" % (event, cur)); continue
    a, b = chain(cur), chain(target)
    lca = next((x for x in a if x in b), None) # lowest common ancestor
    exits = a[:a.index(lca)] if lca else a
    enters = list(reversed(b[:b.index(lca)] if lca else b))
    print("%-6s: %s -> %s | exit %s | enter %s" % (event, cur, target, ",".join(exits), ",".join(enters)))
    cur = target

followUps:
When an event is handled by an ancestor, the transition leaves every state up to, but not including, the lowest common ancestor (LCA), then enters every state down to the target, in that order.

The LCA is the closest state that contains both the source and the target. In the program above, FIRE from DOORS_OPEN to FIRE_RECALL has no common ancestor, so it exits DOORS_OPEN and OPERATIONAL; call from IDLE to MOVING has LCA OPERATIONAL, so it exits IDLE, enters MOVING, and OPERATIONAL is not re-entered. That is what keeps parent state, such as a running timer, intact.

A history state remembers which child was active when you left the parent, so re-entering the parent resumes there instead of at the start.

Model a washing machine with a parent RUNNING containing FILL, WASH, RINSE, SPIN, plus a sibling PAUSED. Pressing pause moves RUNNING to PAUSED and stores the last child, say RINSE. Pressing resume targets RUNNING.history, so the machine returns to RINSE rather than FILL. Without it you would need a copy of PAUSED for every child.

code.title: Random events with invariant checks
code.python:
# Randomized event sequence checking invariants after every step (price 2, coins of 1)
seed = 42
def rnd():                                   # tiny deterministic generator so every run is the same
    global seed
    seed = seed * 48271 % 2147483647
    return seed

stock, credit = 5, 0
coins_in = refunded = sold = violations = 0
for step in range(10000):
    op = rnd() % 3
    if op == 0:                              # insert a coin
        credit += 1; coins_in += 1
    elif op == 1 and credit >= 2 and stock > 0:   # select: guard first, then act
        stock -= 1; credit -= 2; sold += 1
    elif op == 2:                            # cancel: give the credit back
        refunded += credit; credit = 0
    ok = stock >= 0 and credit >= 0 and coins_in == 2 * sold + refunded + credit
    if not ok:
        violations += 1
print("events 10000 sold", sold, "stock", stock, "credit", credit)
print("coins in", coins_in, "= 2*sold +", refunded, "refunded +", credit, "credit")
print("invariant violations:", violations)

followUps:
For the vending machine, assert rules that must hold after every event, whatever the sequence: money is conserved and stock is never negative.

Invariants: stock is at least 0; credit is at least 0; coins in = price x sold + refunded + credit (the program above checks this over 10,000 random events); a product is dispensed only when its slot had stock and enough money was paid; change returned never exceeds the coins in the box; the state is never HAS_MONEY with credit 0, or IDLE with credit above 0; and service is never entered with credit above 0.

AI is good at producing many test cases and odd inputs quickly, but it can write tests that merely repeat the code's behaviour, so you still check that the expected values are right.

Use it to list every (state, event) cell, to draft fault-injection fakes (a bank that drops or duplicates messages) and to write random-sequence generators. Then check three things yourself: the expected result comes from the requirements, not from the implementation; every illegal cell asserts no change; and the test fails when you deliberately break the code (mutation check). Run the tests and read the failures before trusting any of them.

Bugs that appear only under timing, failure or an unusual order of events: a happy-path demo exercises none of them.

Examples: a double sale from a check-then-act race (needs two simultaneous users); a customer charged when the motor jams (needs a failure after payment); an ATM debit retried after a lost reply (needs a network fault); a PIN counter inherited from the previous customer (needs two sessions); an elevator that starves a far floor (needs a long, busy run); and a crash between charging and dispensing. They only surface with fault injection, concurrency tests or random event sequences.

Turn each review question into a test or a build rule so a machine, not memory, catches the problem next time.

Examples: a table test that loops over all (state, event) cells; a lint or architecture test that fails if a state class has a boolean field named isMoving; a fake bank that duplicates and drops messages with an assertion charged == dispensed; a random-sequence test with the invariants; a concurrency test with 100 threads buying the last item that must sell exactly 1; and a check that no lock is held across an I/O call. Run all of them in CI on every pull request, including AI-generated ones.
